g.1: At birth, people are good by nature. By nature they are close to one another; by practice they grow far apart.
g.2: If they are not taught, that nature will change. In the way of teaching, what matters is steady focus.
g.3: Long ago, Mencius's mother chose her neighbours with care. When her son would not study, she cut the cloth on her loom.
g.4: Dou Yanshan had the right way of teaching. He taught his five sons, and every one of them made a name.
g.5: To raise a child without teaching is the father's fault. To teach without strictness is the teacher's neglect.
g.6: For a child not to study is not as it should be. If one does not learn when young, what will one do when old?
g.7: Jade that is not carved does not become a vessel. People who do not learn do not know what is right.
g.8: As a son or daughter, while still young, keep close to teachers and friends and practise good manners.
g.9: Huang Xiang, at nine, warmed his father's bed. Devotion to parents is what everyone should hold to.
g.10: Kong Rong, at four, gave up the bigger pear. Respect for elders should be learned early.
g.11: First, devotion to parents and respect for elder brothers; then, wider knowledge. Learn to count; learn to read.
g.12: One to ten, ten to a hundred, a hundred to a thousand, a thousand to ten thousand.
g.13: The Three Powers are Heaven, Earth and Humankind. The Three Lights are the sun, the moon and the stars.
g.14: The Three Bonds: between ruler and minister, rightness; between father and son, closeness; between husband and wife, harmony.
g.15: Spring and summer, autumn and winter: these four seasons turn without end.
g.16: South and north, west and east: these four directions are reckoned from the centre.
g.17: Water and fire, wood, metal and earth: these Five Phases are rooted in number.
g.18: Benevolence and rightness, propriety, wisdom and good faith: these Five Constants must not be thrown into disorder.
g.19: Rice and sorghum, beans, wheat, broomcorn millet and foxtail millet: these six grains are what people eat.
g.20: Horse, ox and sheep, chicken, dog and pig: these six animals are what people raise.
g.21: Joy and anger, sorrow and fear, love, hate and desire: these seven feelings everyone has.
g.22: Green, red and yellow, black and white: these five colours are what the eye can tell apart.
g.23: Sour, bitter and sweet, pungent and salty: these five tastes are what the mouth can sense.
g.24: Rank, scorched and fragrant, fishy and rotten: these five smells are what the nose can catch.
g.25: Gourd, clay and hide, wood, stone and metal, silk and bamboo: these are the eight sounds.
g.26: The level and the rising, the departing and the entering: these four tones should be kept in harmony.
g.27: Great-great-grandfather, great-grandfather, grandfather, father and oneself; then oneself to son, son to grandson.
g.28: From son and grandson on to great-grandson and great-great-grandson: these are the nine generations, the order of human kinship.
g.29: Between father and son, kindness; between husband and wife, accord. The elder brother is warm, the younger brother respectful.
g.30: Between old and young, due order; between friends, friendship. The ruler is respectful, the minister loyal.
g.31: These ten duties are shared by all people.
g.32: Whoever teaches beginners must take care: explain the words in detail, and make clear where the sentences break.
g.33: Those who study must start at the beginning: finish the Elementary Learning, then go on to the Four Books.
g.34: The Analects has twenty books, in which the disciples recorded the Master's good words.
g.35: The Mencius ends at seven books. It speaks of the Way and virtue, of benevolence and rightness.
g.36: The Doctrine of the Mean came from the brush of Zisi. “Mean” is not leaning; “constant” is not changing.
g.37: The Great Learning was written by Zengzi. It runs from cultivating oneself and ordering one's family to governing the state and bringing peace to the world.
g.38: Once the Classic of Filial Piety is understood and the Four Books are well known, one can begin to read the Six Classics.
g.39: The Odes, the Documents and the Changes, the Rites and the Spring and Autumn are called the Six Classics; they deserve close study.
g.40: There was the Lianshan, there was the Guicang, there was the Zhou Changes: these are the Three Changes, set out in full.
g.41: There are canons and counsels, instructions and announcements, oaths and commands: these are the depths of the Documents.
g.42: Our Duke of Zhou wrote the Rites of Zhou, setting out the six ministries and preserving the framework of government.
g.43: The Elder and Younger Dai annotated the Record of Rites, passing on the sages' words, and ritual and music were made complete.
g.44: The Airs of the States, the Greater and Lesser Elegantiae and the Hymns are called the four parts of the Odes; they should be chanted aloud.
g.45: When the Odes had lost their force, the Spring and Autumn was written, with praise and blame tucked into its wording to tell good from bad.
g.46: The three commentaries are the Gongyang, the Zuo and the Guliang.
g.47: Once the Classics are clear, go on to the philosophers: pick out their main points and remember their stories.
g.48: The five philosophers are Xunzi and Yang Xiong, Wenzhongzi, and Laozi and Zhuangzi.
g.49: With Classics and philosophers mastered, read the histories: trace the lines of succession, and learn how each age began and ended.
g.50: From Fuxi and Shennong to the Yellow Emperor: these are called the Three Sovereigns, and they belong to the remotest past.
g.51: Yao of Tang and Shun of Yu are called the Two Emperors. They yielded the throne to one another with courtesy, and their age is called a golden one.
g.52: Xia had Yu, Shang had Tang, Zhou had Wen and Wu: these are called the Three Kings.
g.53: Xia passed the throne to a son, and the realm became one family's possession. After four hundred years, the altar of Xia was moved.
g.54: Tang overthrew Xia and named his state Shang. After six hundred years it fell under the tyrant Zhou.
g.55: King Wu of Zhou began by putting the tyrant to death. His dynasty lasted eight hundred years, the longest of all.
g.56: When Zhou moved its capital east, the king's authority collapsed. Men trusted in shield and spear and prized the travelling persuaders.
g.57: It began with the Spring and Autumn and ended with the Warring States: the Five Hegemons grew strong, and the Seven Powers arose.
g.58: The Ying house of Qin was the first to swallow up all the states. It passed to a second emperor, and then Chu and Han fought for the realm.
g.59: Gaozu rose and founded the house of Han. Under Emperor Ping, Wang Mang seized the throne.
g.60: Guangwu rose again and founded the Eastern Han. After four hundred years, Han ended with Emperor Xian.
g.61: Wei, Shu and Wu fought over the Han throne. They are called the Three Kingdoms, and they lasted until the two Jin.
g.62: Song and Qi followed, Liang and Chen came after: these were the Southern Dynasties, with their capital at Jinling.
g.63: In the north, the Wei of the Yuan house split into East and West; then came the Zhou of the Yuwen and the Qi of the Gao.
g.64: Then came Sui, which made the land one. It did not last past its second ruler and lost the line of succession.
g.65: Gaozu of Tang raised a righteous army, cleared away the disorder of Sui and laid the foundations of his state.
g.66: Twenty reigns over three hundred years; then Liang destroyed it, and the dynasty changed.
g.67: Liang, Tang and Jin, and then Han and Zhou: these are called the Five Dynasties, and each had a reason for its name.
g.68: The fiery Song arose, receiving the throne from Zhou. Over eighteen reigns, north and south fell into turmoil.
g.69: Liao and Jin both called their rulers emperors. Yuan destroyed Jin and put an end to the Song.
g.70: Its territory was vast, beyond any earlier dynasty, yet after ninety years its mandate was gone.
g.71: Taizu arose and named his state the Great Ming. His reign was called Hongwu, and his capital was Jinling.
g.72: Then the Yongle Emperor moved the capital to Yanjing. Sixteen reigns later came Chongzhen.
g.73: Powerful eunuchs ran riot, rebels were as thick as a forest; Li the Dashing King rose up, and the throne went up in flames.
g.74: Shunzhi of the Qing took the capital. Ten reigns later, Xuantong gave up the throne.
g.75: A president was elected and the republic was made; Han rule was restored over the land, and the Republic of China arose.
g.76: The Twenty-two Histories all are here, recording order and disorder so that we know why states rise and fall.
g.77: Whoever reads history should study the true records, linking past and present as if seeing it with their own eyes.
g.78: Recite it with your mouth and think it through in your mind, in the morning and again at night.
g.79: Long ago Confucius took Xiang Tuo as a teacher. The sages of old still studied hard.
g.80: Zhao, the chief secretary, read the Analects. Though already in high office, he kept studying diligently.
g.81: One copied texts onto woven rushes, another shaved bamboo strips to write on. They had no books, yet still pushed themselves to learn.
g.82: One tied his hair to a roof beam, another jabbed his thigh with an awl. No one made them study; they drove themselves.
g.83: One read by a bag of fireflies, another by the light off the snow. Though their families were poor, they never stopped learning.
g.84: One read while carrying firewood, another hung his book on an ox's horn. Though their bodies were worn out, they still worked hard and stood firm.
g.85: Su Laoquan was twenty-seven when he first resolved to study and set himself to his books.
g.86: Even when he was old, he regretted starting late. You who are young should think of this early.
g.87: Liang Hao was eighty-two when he answered at the palace examination and came first among all the scholars.
g.88: When he succeeded, everyone marvelled. You who are young should set your aim now.
g.89: Ying was eight when he could recite poems; Mi was seven when he could write on the game of go.
g.90: They were quick and bright, and people called them remarkable. You who are studying young should follow their example.
g.91: Cai Wenji could tell the notes of the zither; Xie Daoyun could chant and compose verse.
g.92: They were girls, and yet so clever. You boys should take this as a spur to yourselves.
g.93: Liu Yan of Tang, at just seven, was chosen as a child prodigy and made a text corrector.
g.94: Though he was young, he already held office. You who are studying young can get there too with effort.
g.95: Whoever strives can do the same.
g.96: The dog keeps watch at night, the rooster announces the dawn. If you do not learn, how can you call yourself human?
g.97: The silkworm spins silk, the bee makes honey. People who do not learn fall short even of these creatures.
g.98: Learn when young, act when grown: above, serve your ruler; below, do good to the people.
g.99: Make your name known and bring honour to your parents; add glory to those before you and leave plenty to those after.
g.100: Others leave their children a chest full of gold. I teach my children only one classic.
g.101: Diligence brings results; play brings no profit. Take heed, and put your strength into it.

name.4: A warmed bed and a pear given up
name.16: The Odes and the Spring and Autumn
name.21: From the Spring and Autumn to Qin
name.23: Three Kingdoms to the Northern and Southern Dynasties
name.25: From the Five Dynasties to Song
name.36: Whoever strives can do the same
name.37: The dog keeps watch, the silkworm spins
name.38: Learn when young, act when grown

sum.1: Children start out much alike and end up far apart, and the difference is whether anyone takes them in hand. Mencius's mother took care of the surroundings; Dou Yanshan took care of the principles. Both were parents doing the work themselves, not handing it to someone else. These four groups are one passage; don't split them up.
sum.2: When something goes wrong, first ask whose share it was. These two groups divide the responsibility three ways: the father's, the teacher's and the child's own. It is the only place in the book that names the father, and the only place that puts the father ahead of the child.
sum.3: The first two lectures were about the grown-ups; this one turns to the child: why learning is a must, and why it has to be now. Children grasp the jade comparison at once. The harder part is the next group, where “keep close to teachers and friends” plainly brings teachers and friends into the picture. The share you handed over last time lands here.
sum.4: Being a decent person comes before book learning. Two children, one nine and one four, neither of them much read, yet the book puts them ahead of all learning. The third group, “first devotion to parents, then wider knowledge”, fixes the order: first learn to be a person, then learn your characters.
sum.5: Here the book changes face. Until now it argued; from here on it counts, from one to ten, hanging what a child should know about the world on the numbers. This is a memory frame the old teachers built for children, not filler.
sum.6: Two groups, eight characters, divide the world into time and place. The point is not to recite spring, summer, autumn, winter and north, south, east, west; he already knows those. The point is the last line of each: time goes round in a circle, and place has a centre. Those two lines are the lecture.
sum.7: The Five Phases are baskets for sorting things; the Five Constants are baskets for sorting conduct. Neither is a list; both are ways of classifying. If a child takes them to mean “there are only five things in the world” or “there are only five rules for living”, the lecture has been wasted.
sum.8: The easiest lecture in the book: twelve characters, all things we eat and animals we keep, which the child sees every day. What matters is matching the old names to what is in front of him: foxtail millet is 稷, broomcorn millet is 黍, beans are 菽. Match one, and the lecture comes alive.
sum.9: The seven feelings give names to what is in the heart; the five colours, tastes and smells give names to what three organs take in: eyes, mouth and nose. Together these four groups were the old teachers' first lesson in knowing oneself.
sum.10: Both groups are about sound: one the sound of instruments, one the sound of speech. The eight sounds are not eight pitches but eight materials; an instrument belongs to whatever it is made of. The four tones are the rise and fall of speech, which the child uses every day without being told it has a name.
sum.11: First count out a person's place in the family (the nine generations), then the duty that goes with each place (the ten duties). These five groups are one chain, from great-great-grandfather down to grandson and from father and son up to ruler and minister; cut it in the middle and neither end makes sense. That is why it is the longest lecture in the book and must not be split over two weeks.
sum.12: Before reading, two skills are needed: knowing what words mean, and knowing where a sentence breaks. Children today hardly have to learn either, since their textbooks come with notes and punctuation. So this lecture should let him see that someone did this work for him; it was not always there.
sum.13: Four groups, one book each: the Analects, the Mencius, the Doctrine of the Mean, the Great Learning. It is the most neatly built lecture in the book, and splitting it only confuses. You need not explain what the books say; it is enough to make clear who wrote each one, how long it is and what direction it takes.
sum.14: This lecture hides two cases of “one missing”: it speaks of six classics but names only five, and of three Changes of which only one survives. The missing ones are not misprints; they were lost. What this lecture really teaches is not a list of titles but that books can disappear.
sum.15: The last lecture said which the Six Classics are; this one looks more closely at two of them: what the Documents contain, and who set down the Rites. The Book of Documents is really a collection of state papers in six forms: canons, counsels, instructions, announcements, oaths and commands. A child understands that at once.
sum.16: Two books, two ways of writing. The Odes were sung; the Spring and Autumn was weighed word by word. One asks you to read aloud, the other to look hard. The best way to teach this lecture is to do both on the spot: read one poem aloud, and weigh one word.
sum.17: Only after the Classics come the philosophers, and they are read differently: “pick out the main points and remember the stories”. Grasping the essentials is enough; there is no need to read every word. This is the second way of reading the book teaches, the very opposite of the earlier word-by-word method of explaining terms and marking sentence breaks.
sum.18: Lay a large sheet of paper sideways and draw one long line from left to right. What matters is not getting the names right but getting the lengths right: the Zhou section must be very long, the Qin section only as wide as a fingernail. One look tells the child which was long and which was short, and that is something no amount of reciting can give.
sum.19: History starts here, but the start is legend, not record. Fuxi, Shennong, the Yellow Emperor, Yao and Shun all lived before writing. The historians knew that and still put them first, because there has to be a beginning.
sum.20: Four hundred, six hundred, eight hundred: these three numbers are the only sense of scale in this part, and the child should remember them. Every later dynasty is measured against them: Tang's three hundred years counts as long, Qin's dozen or so as short, all by comparison with these three.
sum.21: The eight-hundred-year Zhou of the last lecture was, in its second half, really in pieces. “The king's authority collapsed” means the Son of Heaven was still there but no one obeyed him. It stayed in pieces for five hundred years until Qin gathered it into one. This lecture is about going from scattered to united.
sum.22: Han was broken once in the middle. Wang Mang took the throne, and a dozen or so years later the Liu family fought its way back. It is the only dynasty that broke and was joined again. The first half is called Western Han, the second Eastern Han, about four hundred years in all.
sum.23: This stretch is chaotic, and the child need not memorise it. A dozen state names pop up in twelve characters, several of them old names used before. The one thing to teach is this: dynasty names get reused, so when you hear one, don't assume; ask which one it is.
sum.24: After more than three hundred years of disorder, Sui gathered the pieces into one and then quickly fell; Tang took over and held on for three hundred years. Sui is uncannily like Qin: each tidied up a broken realm, each was short, and each laid the ground for a long-lived dynasty after it.
sum.25: The five names of the Five Dynasties, Liang, Tang, Jin, Han and Zhou, are all familiar to the child, all used before. That is no accident: each of those five groups chose its name on purpose, hoping to claim kinship with an earlier dynasty and look legitimate. “Each had a reason for its name” says exactly that.
sum.26: The dynasty with the largest territory lived a very short time. “Its territory was vast, beyond any earlier dynasty” stands right next to “after ninety years its mandate was gone”. The contrast is laid out within twelve characters; you need not add much.
sum.27: The man who founded this dynasty had herded cattle as a boy, lived as a monk and begged for food. What matters most in this lecture is not the Ming but this man, because he ties back to the book's first line: by nature close, by practice far apart. Similar starting points, very different endings.
sum.28: The book ends here, but more than a hundred years followed. It is not that the book was left unfinished; whoever writes a book can only write up to the day they are living in. That is the most important sentence of this lecture.
sum.29: After eleven weeks of dynasties, this lecture looks back and asks: what is the use of reading all this, and how should it be read? The answer is six characters: recite with the mouth, think with the mind. Say it aloud, and think it over.
sum.30: Even Confucius took a seven-year-old as his teacher; even a man who became chief minister kept reading at home. This part of the book begins here on purpose: first show that people who are already accomplished still learn, so that the poor, the old and the young of the next nine lectures can stand on firm ground.
sum.32: Four people: one read by firefly light, one by the glow of snow, one while carrying firewood, one with his book hung on an ox's horn. The point is not these four tricks but the idea of finding a way when there seems to be none.
sum.33: Late is not too late. The two pairs, four groups, are taught together because they say the same thing: one man began studying only at twenty-seven, another is said to have come first in the examinations at eighty-two.
sum.34: Two people about your child's age: Zu Ying wrote poems at eight, Li Mi wrote on the game of go at seven. The weight of this lecture is in their ages. The people in the last lecture were too old; these are the same age as he is.
sum.35: Of the book's 101 groups, this is the only one whose heroes are women. Both were real people, and both stories are easy to tell. The hard part is the second half: “They were girls, and yet so clever; you boys should take this as a spur.” Today that line cannot be taught at face value.
sum.36: One last example, then a single line gathers up everything before it: whoever strives can do the same. From Confucius to seven-year-old Liu Yan, seven lectures and a dozen or so people all come down to these six characters.
sum.37: After seven lectures about people, this one suddenly turns to animals: the dog keeps watch at night, the rooster crows, the silkworm spins silk, the bee makes honey. Each does its one thing, and each gets it done. It is the plainest comparison in the book and the easiest lecture to understand.
sum.38: What learning is for. Three groups push outward step by step: first do your work well, then make life better for those around you, and finally leave something for those who come after. The last group is where these lecture notes come from: others leave their child a chest of gold; I leave mine a classic.
sum.39: One group, twelve characters, and the year is done. This lecture teaches nothing new. Read the whole text through once from the beginning, then write your child a letter and paste it on the last page of the booklet. This lecture is a ceremony, not a lesson.

yw.11: Wang Xiang's edition writes 弟 for 悌 (“respect for elder brothers”); the two characters were used interchangeably.
yw.22: Not in Wang Xiang's edition. The three groups on colours, tastes and smells were added in later popular editions; the lecture notes follow those.
yw.23: Not in Wang Xiang's edition (added later, see group 22).
yw.24: Not in Wang Xiang's edition (added later, see group 22).
yw.26: Not in Wang Xiang's edition. The group on the four tones was added in later popular editions; the lecture notes follow those.
yw.28: Wang Xiang's edition writes 元 for 玄 (“great-great-”), because Qing-dynasty writers avoided 玄, part of the Kangxi Emperor's personal name (Xuanye).
yw.32: Wang Xiang's edition writes 詁 for 故 (“meanings of words”); the two were used interchangeably.
yw.69: Not in Wang Xiang's edition. His history stops at the Song (“The fiery Song arose … north and south fell into turmoil”) and goes straight on to the Seventeen Histories. The seven groups from Liao and Jin through Yuan, Ming and Qing to the Republic were added by later hands; the lecture notes follow the popular editions.
